Press Release:


Trevor Noah: A Carte Blanche Special
In 2014, Trevor Noah was just a well-known stand-up comedian with a recurring role as a contributor on one of the biggest talk shows in the
USA. Now at 33 years old, Noah is taking on the Big Apple in a big way. His path from apartheid South Africa to the anchor chair of The Daily
Show is the stuff of dreams. As he briefly returns home with a best-selling book already in the bag and sold-out shows around the country, Carte
Blanche takes you behind the scenes into the New York life of South Africa’s favourite export.
Producer: Diana

Script:


Trevor: Heh Heh……Heh

V/O
It’s no exaggeration to call Trevor Noah South Africa’s comic wunderkind

Trevor: When a black person…Eish.

From his early twenties his stand ups were already a sell out…his comedy specials a total hit….. In 2011 Trevor started to test the comedy waters further afield.

Trevor: You know Red carpets sound like fun…. Bedroom wall because cool…. APPLAUSE

V/O
Two years ago aged only thirty one Trevor struck comedy gold when he followed Jon Stewart becoming the host of The Daily Show …One of America’s highest rated satirical late night shows.

Trevor: I’ve never seen that many flashes in my life……Pose.

V/O
Carte Blanche got to meet with Trevor in New York for an exclusive one on one interview….

Devi: Only send me on the Hectic stories
Devi: Trevor they only send me on the hectic stories so clearly there has to be another agenda right…truth of the matter is//
You are here because of Joshua Door they want the money…I knew this was going to happen you bought these couches Trevor and then you pull out the numbers hit the camera…I never thought they were going to come the couches are very comfortable
I didn’t even want that love seat for my self

V/O
Trevor has taken South African stand up comedy onto the international stage.

Devi: We all knew T going to America…SA’s wishing you well
I did feel a lot of people supporting me I did feel a lot of people saying Hey you are doing something we have never seen before and I know that because of people who did comedy before me I got to be at a certain level and I hoped that I would open the door for other people to take it to the next step after me.

Trevor Up sound Thank you very much…thi is us

Trevor: I always tell people now when I walk through the streets, when I perform anywhere in the world I carry the fire of SA with me. I go like no guys I have a country where they told me I’m a star so I can meet you here in America and you can go like we don’t even know you, that’s your problem that’s your problem there is a place where they told me I am someone.

Devi: Did you set your sights on TDS?
I don’t think I ever set my sights on the daily show because TDS It wasn’t a real thing in my world, I knew of Jon Stewart I knew of what he was doing but I never thought to my self It was something I was going to do because I didn’t think it was something I could do.

Link
Trevor Noah might be seen as a satirist a comic genius but the reality is a lot of what he says is based on authenticity and reality, perhaps that’s why he is so successful

V/O
Trevor’s mother is Xhosa his father, Swiss…..In South Africa in the 80’s his very birth was a crime, his existence problematic which ever side of the apartheid fence you were. In his words, never fitting in anywhere gave him the ability to live nowhere and everywhere and its these memories much of his comedy is based on.

TREVOR: To give you a bit of a back story… Dammit

Devi: Like for you growing up in SA as a coloured guy?
I don’t think I ever grew up as a coloured guy I lived with my Mom in a coloured area called Eden Park which was next to Thokoza. What was funny was I mean my Mom was black Xhosa woman through and through so no one assumed anything but now I was in a coloured neighbourhood so everyone would come up to me and start speaking and I didn’t really speak Afrikaans that well and kids would come up to me Ek se braa…. I don’t …OK you think you’re special jy is high buck and I don’t know what this is so I was in this world where people assume I was something that I wasn’t and I would spend a lot of time explaining why I was speaking Zulu and not Afrikaans
Devi: It’s a difficult thing for people to get there heads around because we do put people into compartments even now?
I enjoyed it I played games with it some people would speak vernacular around me not knowing that I understood it you know what I mean I would be at Checkers at the till and some woman would be saying something about me and then I would respond in Zulu ….sorry boetie…collard even if I am coloured why would you say…it’s the fun side of South Africa. Everyone slowly coming to a place where cultures where mixing where they couldn’t previously.

GRANDMOTHER Gogo I got my height from her
This is where I grew up

Devi: But you’re grandmother never beat you up because you were lighter skinned?
Right my grandmother was afraid …she saw my mom when my mom would hit me my grandmother was like No No No you cant beat this white child… my mom was like this child is not white this child is from this house we beat him you know what I am saying my grandmother was like he going to break now what you saying now you beating a white child he’s going to break my mom was like no I am going to break him…he doesn’t listen because I was so naughty.
Devi: I can kinda see this I am an ex high school teacher
You see naughty in my eyes.


Trevor Part 2: 10 53 sec

Trevor this is the where I grew up…this is the toilet…sorry

Trevor: I remember when we were growing up you’re living in Orlando East you’re seeing people around you working to get by, you are seeing people struggling but not suffering you see them choosing to not suffer, I remember seeing building a gate but they didn’t even have a wall and then you are like you don’t even have a car but you’re building a driveway and that was always a beautiful world to live I to be in a place where people in some ways believed their lives could and would become better even if they couldn’t see it right then and there.
Devi: And always a drive way
Always you had to have a drive way no car or if you had a car on the bricks no wheels one day the wheels are coming then the engine then we are on.

LINK
Trevor has inherited his mother’s talent of walking on the sunny side of the street but that’s easy to say when you’re living the American dream not easy when you’re living a secret in Soweto and can’t even call your father Dad in public

Trevor: Initially I saw my father as much as we cold see my father considering the laws in South Africa apartheid after that ended I got to see him a lot more but my mother and I because we had lived for so long I don’t think my mom ever wanted to let go of that independence we maintained a relationship and I was really lucky because as much as there are things I didn’t get in terms of time I still got to know him and I still got to experience him in my life in my formative years which is very important. You know when I made contact with him again I met my father and you realise time is what has separated you but there is still a love that connects the two of you.

TREVOR: Every thing with him…

Devi: What did you inherit from your Dad?
Trevor: That’s interesting the biggest thing I inherited from my father was what my Mom inherited from his as well and that was a pragmatism and an appreciation of money. My mom always used to say the biggest curse we black people have is we don’t know how to save money. But she was not like that in the beginning my dad was the one who said to her Man you just spend all your money ad my mom said Ya because its my money and he said what about tomorrow what about the next day as a first generation its very difficult to absorb that responsibility so that’s the biggest thing I inherited from my dad.

Devi: But she had this plan it seems that was just to expose you to just about everything?
Trevor: Right, my mother gave me the gift of seeing the world, I remember my mom would drive me to Houghton just to see rich peoples houses, we would go and stand and look over the walls and she would drive me to high points where we could see the whole of the city. She would take me to places where I could see what life could be like and not just moneywise but so you could see your world is not what you think it is. ….. the things of white people she would give me books she would give me opinions and ideas because those are the tools you need to give your child because even if they cannot access it the knowledge of it gives you a goal.

Devi: How were you with the ladies at school?
Trevor: Horrible Horrible
Devi: Because you see you really charming?
Trevor: Charming where?
Devi: At school
Trevor: There was no charming at school
Devi: How Trevor
School I had a lot of friends at school I was fairly liked I had a lot of friends, I avoided conflict but No charming I was afraid of women.
Devi: Why
Trevor: Because you don’t want to get rejected skin as I teenager, pimples that were popping on my neck.
Devi: That bad?
Trevor: People were like what happened here and you would be like that’s my face….and a lot of kids go through that and you would think that’s the worst time of your life you want to kill yourself you don’t want to go to school kids are laughing at you kids are pointing at your face
Devi: Have you become a lot more confident?
Trevor: I’ve worked on it…

Up sound I have those …..

V/O
Trevor’s comic career was not planned…in his early twenties he was at the comedy club, Horror Cafe in Newtown Johannesburg when his cousin pushed him on to the stage.

Trevor: I got on to the stage and I stood there and then a friend of mine shouted from the audience Tell them that story from that other day.
Devi: They are reminding you of your material?
Trevor: But I didn’t know it was material I just thought it was stories and I told a story and the audience laughed and then I told another one and they laughed
Devi: Did you like that feeling?
It was great and still is I like making people feel good.

V/O
When Trevor wrote his book’ Born a Crime’ he didn’t hide the abuse his mother sufferesf at the hands of her ex partner.

Devi: You have always been very upfront about the abusive relationship your mom had with her former partner, why did you make that decision that you were going to tell that story?
Trevor: Because I realised I didn’t have to be nor did my family have to be ashamed I spent so much time even when I was growing up being ashamed being embarrassed that I grew up in a house where my mom was being hit you want to hide it you don’t want anyone to know not realising that many of your friends are going through the same thing not realising you are growing up in a society where many people are experiencing the same thing.
Devi: Because that was normal?
Trevor: Exactly it still is in many places and its not different in America…I think in America it is once every 30 seconds a woman is a victim of domestic abuse the reason I spoke about it in the book I didn’t want people to have the impression that I had some perfect life I didn’t. I didn’t want people to have the impression that you can’t get out from under it I also used to have the attitude of but why don’t you just leave mom, why does she stay, people always say that about a woman because clearly than she wants it and then you start to realise the complexities of life and of love and the world you live in you realise that it is a lot more difficult than we would like it to be.

V/O
…. in 2010 Trevor began to set his sights on a more international arena.

Trevor: If you think you are at the top then you should be finding the place where you are at the bottom

TREVOR JOKE Thr number one

Devi: Where you nervous in front of your first international audience?
Trevor: I was horrible, first time I did an international audience I was in England I went to do a show and I got on stage I will never forget this I said Hello my Name is Trevor Noah and I am from SA Booo and some guy didn’t even know me he was like get off the stage I panicked and the next gig was horrible and then again…
Devi: So what happens when you do three shows in a row and they bomb?
Trevor: I was lucky I as there with a friend good fellow comedian David Kibuuka and we sat down the next day with a pen and paper and we started working through the jokes and we said we will make this better we will find a way to make this funnier and you sit for hours and that’s the hard work now just writing out what you.re trying to do it and how your going to do it.

V/O
And they did, Trevor’s stand up comedy routine grew internationally. Pretty soon he was making appearances on American Late night talk shows and British panel shows,

Devi: When you first came to NY…this is an expensive place, what was it like for you, where did you stay, with friends in digs, did you drink one bottle of water the entire day did you eat all your meals…
Trevor: I didn’t come to NY first I don’t think I would have ever afforded it when I first came to USA I moved to California, I lived with a friend of mine there I lived in a very small apartment and I used all the money I had in SA. so I said what is the one thing I want to invest in is myself, I didn’t get paid for I think 7 or 8 months I lived and you have to eat and you’re buying sandwiches now that are R200 you’re still using rand in your head because you are paying in rand and now you’re going aw man I wish I had some Pronutro or something that I could fill up with water to get full all I could do was put my head down and work.
Devi: Some people would have said 6, 3 months into it that’s it moneys running out I need to get the gigs, you stuck in there.
Trevor: Ya because I believed in myself and I also saw progress don’t get me wrong I am not a crazy person. If I was here for 3 months and I saw nothing I would have left as well you mustn’t be one of those people who believes in J and jeh and and it never ends and now you’re believing and there’s nothing and now you’re believing and you’re homeless No you should still be reasonable chase your dreams but be reasonable, I saw that I was getting more shows I saw that I was getting booked more still wasn’t getting paid but I saw that there was an improvement here was a chance there was an opportunity and I thought then I can stay because the re was an end goal in sight.

Trevor Part 3

Trevor: As some of you may or may not know I have a new job….. it isn t a job.

Link
In 2014 Trevor Noah made 2 appearances as a contributor on the Daily Show and just 18 months later it was announced that he would be replacing long standing host John Stewart….

V/O
It all started with a call from the man himself….

Devi: He didn’t just call you out of the blue?
He did call me out of the blue, he just called me like you guys call people and say where is the money that’s what he did just out of the blue private number Hello and then JS I don’t know if you know me I aid of course I know you I want you to come work with me.
Devi: When he says you should come do something with me on the show you are like…for real when today?
Trevor: You know what s nice is one thing I really enjoyed when I first came to the Daily Show is you know…It’s a big organisation but at the same time it feels really small. So it was me hanging out with this man who I got along with and we became friends and we were laughing and having fun and we realised we are comedians who see the world in a similar way but from different points of view and so in the conversation and in the laughing he said Why don’t you …
Devi: Pull in
Trevor: Yes, pull in and that’s what it is….
Devi: You pulled in and stayed
Devi: You’re Trevor you’re ours you belong to us.
Trevor: I thought it was going to be I will always come and visit the show when I am in town. Then Jon Stewart announced he was leaving.
Devi: Did you think you were in with a chance? Because you are not American you have a whole other different background?
No I didn’t I approached it the same way I used to play lotto, choose my numbers, No I am not going to win you just put my ticket in the ashtray and you carry on with your life. I am not from the place where I think people will be chosen and I understand I am a strange choice. and that’s half of what life is for me I don’t expect anything but I will still put the work in to try because if you don’t try you can never get anything.

V/O
On the 28th September, 2015, Trevor took over the chair, his first night as host of The Daily Show.

Up Sound Before we get started……

Devi: You are the boss the buck stops with you?
Trevor: Yes…
Devi: They sue you.
Trevor: Basically I am the Guptas and everyone else is my Zumas they have to do what I say…

Link
If you walk down West 52 Street Hells Kitchen New York you would be forgiven if you missed that white door its quiet unimpressive but behind that door that’s where the Daily Show is put together.

V/O
`We spent time behind the scenes of The Daily Show, talking to the fans, seeing how their script writers and producers put the show together. Whilst the organisation is big the feeling is intimate even pets are welcomed in this space.

Vox Pop

V/O
This Emmy award winning late night comedy talk show is all about their take on what’s happening in the news and the one constant is the morning meeting.

Link
Monday to Thursday the day starts at 9 am with a script writers meeting for scriptwriters where basically ideas are thrown around but the content will shape the evenings show

Devi: How do you stay on top of it the news cycle is never ending.
Trevor: I enjoy it you know again in a similar way I am connected to what it was like in South Africa as SA’s we take for granted how political we are on a base level so when I first came to America people said are you political and I said No I am not but then I realised what we think is not political in SA people here would think is revolutionary. Many Americans do not engage in politics at all but that’s changed now because of Donald Trump now everyone speaks about politics everyone is.

Vox pop

Devi: What was that first couple of weeks like because people were quiet critical others were quiet supportive?
Trevor: You know the first couple of weeks were interesting because running a show is a very difficult exercise you know people take for granted it’s not hosting… I am used to hosting shows when I worked with M-Net on my show back in SA I was lucky I had started to experience what it was like to run a show so hiring writers and working with the actual production of what you are doing working through the editing etc but nothing on this scale so it was tough on the inside I didn’t have time to focus on what ws happening on the outside.

V/O
Midday every day, Trevor begins to review and refine the headline jokes. Around 4 in the afternoon there is rehearsal….An hour is left for rewrites until the taping of the show somewhere between 6 and 7 pm in front of a live studio audience.

Link
Here on the set of the Daily Show just over 200 audience members fill these seats Monday to Thursday.

V/O
And so every day in snow or a heat wave by 3 pm the line starts for wanna be audience members who haven’t got one of the 200 or so free tickets but are hoping for a no show….. we even found some South Africans in the line

Vox Pop

Devi: So the audience seems to have stabilised and you are attracting a younger audience and that’s a tough thing to do?
Trevor; Yes that was the goal from the beginning, it was scary because the network said to us we want younger viewers but younger viewers don’t watch TV any more so what do you do…I had to set about doing creating a show that I believed would be interesting to people of different walks of life and ages.
Devi: How different is an American audience to a SA audience
Trevor: Very different… one thing is that Americans are in a space where there are a lot of conversations that are taken a lot more seriously in America than they are in SA we have many similarities don’t get me wrong you know in SA we are a lot more brash and way more honest in SA we just tell people how we feel and what we think and Americans are a lot more delicate and beat about the bush.

Vox Pop

V/O
Trump’s presidency has been a boon for American comedy and satire…. The President only has to open his mouth…or send a tweet and there is a relentless barrage of media….Trump might be an easy target but this also means comedy has more political power than ever before for keeping the pressure on the ~President

Devi: You’ve had practice you have had President Zuma
Trevor: Definitely you know one thing I like about working on TDS now is that Donald Trump in many ways reminds me of JZ

Trevor: UP SOUND

Trevor …. both Presidents who are doing their best thing living their best life and you know people love them people hate them they both have many wives you know are not afraid of being themselves not fans of the media…there is many similarities and parallels you can draw I feel like in many ways I am familiar with the leader who is DT because he reminds me of people that we know back home.
Devi: Have you extended an invite to Pres Tump
Trevor: Oh yeah but we have been rejected many times
Devi: You mean he even replies?
Well his people reply for him it’s a NO but we keep asking week in and week out

Devi: Do you sometimes sit here and pinch your self
Trevor: All the time especially when I walk to work when I leave at night I don’t take any of this for granted it was never promised to me and neither is tomorrow but I am blessed that I have this today I am lucky that I have this job and its an amazing job and I get to do this every single day of my life so I don’t take that for granted at all

Trevor Part 4

Devi: Nice pozzie I have to say …doorman everything.
Trevor: Its funny when you move to the US you realise how many things we take for granted in SA. The space we have the type of lifestyle you can live for the amount of money you can live it and then you come to NY and you have to live a lot smaller but at the same time you’re in NY city.

V/O
Trevor Noah has only recently upgraded from renting to buying his New York penthouse …. for a man who works non stops it made sense to buy juts a few blocks from the The Daily Show studio.

Devi And works just down the road?
Trevor Yes
Devi: That for me is the best part
Trevor: The thing is NY traffic is insane so when I first moved here I realised the traffic was insane and in the winter time its snow so I dint know how to walk in the snow I still don’t know how to walk in the snow.

Devi: and Your mom is she planning a trip?
Trevor: My mom for what…
Devi:For you
Trevor: I must come home…you going to NY you will come home what am I doing in America No
Devi: Picture her here have to entertain her
Trevor: But I wouldn’t have to entertain her she does her own thing…walk…my mom has always been a free spirit that’s the nice thing about my family we talk we keep in contact but everyone is very easy in terms where we will bump into each other in the world

TREVOR: I got so home sick….

Devi: Advice for young SA’s who are watching the show?
The biggest advice for young SA’s is they have to break the curses of the previous generations they have to work hard not to inherit the resentments and hatreds of the previous generations. Young SA have to build whilst acknowledging the foundations of their country may be shaky,. Young SA’s have to realise its work and sometimes I think that was a message that was never given to us when 94 came and when freedom came. They said free houses for all free everything but people don’t realise that freedom is hard work I used to complain about my Mom like she was the government oppressing me. Aah this lady tells me when to sleep ha ha she doesn’t want to give me money this women telling me I must turn off the lights turn on the lights I must clean the yard I am a prisoner, a prisoner and then she said go and be free in the world and there I was going with the electricity bill I have t turn off the lights I have to pay for water pay the rent and I have to clean the house and then I realise freedom is hard work and a lot of people say they want freedom but what they are actually saying is they just don’t want to have accountability and there is a difference.

Trevor Joke

V/O
Stand up comedy is still Trevor’s love, it’s the rapport with the audience, the often unscripted moments, and to feed his passion most weekends he travels to gigs sometimes in America sometimes further afield.

Trevor’s won a number of international awards already…and just last week he received the Comedy Person of the Year Award at the ‘Just for Laughs’ Comedy Fest in Montreal.

Trevor: I love stand up comedy I still love it today I been blessed enough to do it all over the world, its not easy to go from Germany to America to UK to Australia to SA not easy at all but that’s where the hard work comes in but a lot of the time people don’t see the the hard work. So they see you and go even me. I must do that but its Ya but you don’t see the work.
Devi: Explain that to people they think its glamourous, we’ve shown the glamour been on set with you jump into helicopter James Bonds style its all going to be fantastic, but that’s what people see is are you getting enough sleep at night how hard are you working…
Trevor:. People say WOW overnight Ya but what was happening at night I eas working and that’s where you remember to remind yourself of what your goal is and these very difficult times that come with it. But if you pace yourself and if you see life as a whole instead of little moments where your emotions are going u and down you have a broader understanding of what’s happening to you.

Devi: Are you living the dream now.
Trevor: Can I tell you it took me a long time to realise that that I was always living the dream. If you’re waiting to live the dream you will never live the dream. Be happy in the space that you’re in and then everything else comes to you. It’s a strange concept because people always go if I can just get the car then I will be happy; If I can just get the job then I will be happy; No be happy then let those things come to you otherwise you are mortgaging your happiness for the future.

V/O
This week Trevor will be back in South Africa for a series of specials and stand up comedy acts.

Devi: What do you miss most about SA
The people, I miss the people I miss how polite we are, how we laugh. I miss how loud we are. I miss our…the fact that we greet hello when you walk in the room. People don’t greet in America they walk right past each into rooms out of rooms they don’t care, they don’t see each other Sawubone I see you that’s all.

Up sound: Have you seen…selfie monster

Devi: They sent me to NY every women check if dimples are real I just want to touch one……..we had women swooning outside
Trevor: I inherited these from my father, there’s something else……full Trevor smile.

December 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 06 December 2017 06 August 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 30 August 2017 Press Release: Trevor Noah: A Carte Blanche Special In 2014, Trevor Noah was just a well-known stand-up comedian with a recurring role as a contributor on one of the biggest talk shows in the USA. Now at 33 years old, Noah is taking on the Big Apple in a big way. His path from apartheid South Africa to the anchor chair of The Daily Show is the stuff of dreams. As he briefly returns home with a best-selling book already in the bag and sold-out shows around the country, Carte Blanche takes you behind the scenes into the New York life of South Africa’s favourite export. Producer: Diana Script: Trevor: Heh Heh……Heh V/O It’s no exaggeration to call Trevor Noah South Africa’s comic wunderkind Trevor: When a black person…Eish. From his early twenties his stand ups were already a sell out…his comedy specials a total hit….. In 2011 Trevor started to test the comedy waters further afield. Trevor: You know Red carpets sound like fun…. Bedroom wall because cool…. APPLAUSE V/O Two years ago aged only thirty one Trevor struck comedy gold when he followed Jon Stewart becoming the host of The Daily Show …One of America’s highest rated satirical late night shows. Trevor: I’ve never seen that many flashes in my life……Pose. V/O Carte Blanche got to meet with Trevor in New York for an exclusive one on one interview…. Devi: Only send me on the Hectic stories Devi: Trevor they only send me on the hectic stories so clearly there has to be another agenda right…truth of the matter is// You are here because of Joshua Door they want the money…I knew this was going to happen you bought these couches Trevor and then you pull out the numbers hit the camera…I never thought they were going to come the couches are very comfortable I didn’t even want that love seat for my self V/O Trevor has taken South African stand up comedy onto the international stage. Devi: We all knew T going to America…SA’s wishing you well I did feel a lot of people supporting me I did feel a lot of people saying Hey you are doing something we have never seen before and I know that because of people who did comedy before me I got to be at a certain level and I hoped that I would open the door for other people to take it to the next step after me. Trevor Up sound Thank you very much…thi is us Trevor: I always tell people now when I walk through the streets, when I perform anywhere in the world I carry the fire of SA with me. I go like no guys I have a country where they told me I’m a star so I can meet you here in America and you can go like we don’t even know you, that’s your problem that’s your problem there is a place where they told me I am someone. Devi: Did you set your sights on TDS? I don’t think I ever set my sights on the daily show because TDS It wasn’t a real thing in my world, I knew of Jon Stewart I knew of what he was doing but I never thought to my self It was something I was going to do because I didn’t think it was something I could do. Link Trevor Noah might be seen as a satirist a comic genius but the reality is a lot of what he says is based on authenticity and reality, perhaps that’s why he is so successful V/O Trevor’s mother is Xhosa his father, Swiss…..In South Africa in the 80’s his very birth was a crime, his existence problematic which ever side of the apartheid fence you were. In his words, never fitting in anywhere gave him the ability to live nowhere and everywhere and its these memories much of his comedy is based on. TREVOR: To give you a bit of a back story… Dammit Devi: Like for you growing up in SA as a coloured guy? I don’t think I ever grew up as a coloured guy I lived with my Mom in a coloured area called Eden Park which was next to Thokoza. What was funny was I mean my Mom was black Xhosa woman through and through so no one assumed anything but now I was in a coloured neighbourhood so everyone would come up to me and start speaking and I didn’t really speak Afrikaans that well and kids would come up to me Ek se braa…. I don’t …OK you think you’re special jy is high buck and I don’t know what this is so I was in this world where people assume I was something that I wasn’t and I would spend a lot of time explaining why I was speaking Zulu and not Afrikaans Devi: It’s a difficult thing for people to get there heads around because we do put people into compartments even now? I enjoyed it I played games with it some people would speak vernacular around me not knowing that I understood it you know what I mean I would be at Checkers at the till and some woman would be saying something about me and then I would respond in Zulu ….sorry boetie…collard even if I am coloured why would you say…it’s the fun side of South Africa. Everyone slowly coming to a place where cultures where mixing where they couldn’t previously. GRANDMOTHER Gogo I got my height from her This is where I grew up Devi: But you’re grandmother never beat you up because you were lighter skinned? Right my grandmother was afraid …she saw my mom when my mom would hit me my grandmother was like No No No you cant beat this white child… my mom was like this child is not white this child is from this house we beat him you know what I am saying my grandmother was like he going to break now what you saying now you beating a white child he’s going to break my mom was like no I am going to break him…he doesn’t listen because I was so naughty. Devi: I can kinda see this I am an ex high school teacher You see naughty in my eyes. Trevor Part 2: 10 53 sec Trevor this is the where I grew up…this is the toilet…sorry Trevor: I remember when we were growing up you’re living in Orlando East you’re seeing people around you working to get by, you are seeing people struggling but not suffering you see them choosing to not suffer, I remember seeing building a gate but they didn’t even have a wall and then you are like you don’t even have a car but you’re building a driveway and that was always a beautiful world to live I to be in a place where people in some ways believed their lives could and would become better even if they couldn’t see it right then and there. Devi: And always a drive way Always you had to have a drive way no car or if you had a car on the bricks no wheels one day the wheels are coming then the engine then we are on. LINK Trevor has inherited his mother’s talent of walking on the sunny side of the street but that’s easy to say when you’re living the American dream not easy when you’re living a secret in Soweto and can’t even call your father Dad in public Trevor: Initially I saw my father as much as we cold see my father considering the laws in South Africa apartheid after that ended I got to see him a lot more but my mother and I because we had lived for so long I don’t think my mom ever wanted to let go of that independence we maintained a relationship and I was really lucky because as much as there are things I didn’t get in terms of time I still got to know him and I still got to experience him in my life in my formative years which is very important. You know when I made contact with him again I met my father and you realise time is what has separated you but there is still a love that connects the two of you. TREVOR: Every thing with him… Devi: What did you inherit from your Dad? Trevor: That’s interesting the biggest thing I inherited from my father was what my Mom inherited from his as well and that was a pragmatism and an appreciation of money. My mom always used to say the biggest curse we black people have is we don’t know how to save money. But she was not like that in the beginning my dad was the one who said to her Man you just spend all your money ad my mom said Ya because its my money and he said what about tomorrow what about the next day as a first generation its very difficult to absorb that responsibility so that’s the biggest thing I inherited from my dad. Devi: But she had this plan it seems that was just to expose you to just about everything? Trevor: Right, my mother gave me the gift of seeing the world, I remember my mom would drive me to Houghton just to see rich peoples houses, we would go and stand and look over the walls and she would drive me to high points where we could see the whole of the city. She would take me to places where I could see what life could be like and not just moneywise but so you could see your world is not what you think it is. ….. the things of white people she would give me books she would give me opinions and ideas because those are the tools you need to give your child because even if they cannot access it the knowledge of it gives you a goal. Devi: How were you with the ladies at school? Trevor: Horrible Horrible Devi: Because you see you really charming? Trevor: Charming where? Devi: At school Trevor: There was no charming at school Devi: How Trevor School I had a lot of friends at school I was fairly liked I had a lot of friends, I avoided conflict but No charming I was afraid of women. Devi: Why Trevor: Because you don’t want to get rejected skin as I teenager, pimples that were popping on my neck. Devi: That bad? Trevor: People were like what happened here and you would be like that’s my face….and a lot of kids go through that and you would think that’s the worst time of your life you want to kill yourself you don’t want to go to school kids are laughing at you kids are pointing at your face Devi: Have you become a lot more confident? Trevor: I’ve worked on it… Up sound I have those ….. V/O Trevor’s comic career was not planned…in his early twenties he was at the comedy club, Horror Cafe in Newtown Johannesburg when his cousin pushed him on to the stage. Trevor: I got on to the stage and I stood there and then a friend of mine shouted from the audience Tell them that story from that other day. Devi: They are reminding you of your material? Trevor: But I didn’t know it was material I just thought it was stories and I told a story and the audience laughed and then I told another one and they laughed Devi: Did you like that feeling? It was great and still is I like making people feel good. V/O When Trevor wrote his book’ Born a Crime’ he didn’t hide the abuse his mother sufferesf at the hands of her ex partner. Devi: You have always been very upfront about the abusive relationship your mom had with her former partner, why did you make that decision that you were going to tell that story? Trevor: Because I realised I didn’t have to be nor did my family have to be ashamed I spent so much time even when I was growing up being ashamed being embarrassed that I grew up in a house where my mom was being hit you want to hide it you don’t want anyone to know not realising that many of your friends are going through the same thing not realising you are growing up in a society where many people are experiencing the same thing. Devi: Because that was normal? Trevor: Exactly it still is in many places and its not different in America…I think in America it is once every 30 seconds a woman is a victim of domestic abuse the reason I spoke about it in the book I didn’t want people to have the impression that I had some perfect life I didn’t. I didn’t want people to have the impression that you can’t get out from under it I also used to have the attitude of but why don’t you just leave mom, why does she stay, people always say that about a woman because clearly than she wants it and then you start to realise the complexities of life and of love and the world you live in you realise that it is a lot more difficult than we would like it to be. V/O …. in 2010 Trevor began to set his sights on a more international arena. Trevor: If you think you are at the top then you should be finding the place where you are at the bottom TREVOR JOKE Thr number one Devi: Where you nervous in front of your first international audience? Trevor: I was horrible, first time I did an international audience I was in England I went to do a show and I got on stage I will never forget this I said Hello my Name is Trevor Noah and I am from SA Booo and some guy didn’t even know me he was like get off the stage I panicked and the next gig was horrible and then again… Devi: So what happens when you do three shows in a row and they bomb? Trevor: I was lucky I as there with a friend good fellow comedian David Kibuuka and we sat down the next day with a pen and paper and we started working through the jokes and we said we will make this better we will find a way to make this funnier and you sit for hours and that’s the hard work now just writing out what you.re trying to do it and how your going to do it. V/O And they did, Trevor’s stand up comedy routine grew internationally. Pretty soon he was making appearances on American Late night talk shows and British panel shows, Devi: When you first came to NY…this is an expensive place, what was it like for you, where did you stay, with friends in digs, did you drink one bottle of water the entire day did you eat all your meals… Trevor: I didn’t come to NY first I don’t think I would have ever afforded it when I first came to USA I moved to California, I lived with a friend of mine there I lived in a very small apartment and I used all the money I had in SA. so I said what is the one thing I want to invest in is myself, I didn’t get paid for I think 7 or 8 months I lived and you have to eat and you’re buying sandwiches now that are R200 you’re still using rand in your head because you are paying in rand and now you’re going aw man I wish I had some Pronutro or something that I could fill up with water to get full all I could do was put my head down and work. Devi: Some people would have said 6, 3 months into it that’s it moneys running out I need to get the gigs, you stuck in there. Trevor: Ya because I believed in myself and I also saw progress don’t get me wrong I am not a crazy person. If I was here for 3 months and I saw nothing I would have left as well you mustn’t be one of those people who believes in J and jeh and and it never ends and now you’re believing and there’s nothing and now you’re believing and you’re homeless No you should still be reasonable chase your dreams but be reasonable, I saw that I was getting more shows I saw that I was getting booked more still wasn’t getting paid but I saw that there was an improvement here was a chance there was an opportunity and I thought then I can stay because the re was an end goal in sight. Trevor Part 3 Trevor: As some of you may or may not know I have a new job….. it isn t a job. Link In 2014 Trevor Noah made 2 appearances as a contributor on the Daily Show and just 18 months later it was announced that he would be replacing long standing host John Stewart…. V/O It all started with a call from the man himself…. Devi: He didn’t just call you out of the blue? He did call me out of the blue, he just called me like you guys call people and say where is the money that’s what he did just out of the blue private number Hello and then JS I don’t know if you know me I aid of course I know you I want you to come work with me. Devi: When he says you should come do something with me on the show you are like…for real when today? Trevor: You know what s nice is one thing I really enjoyed when I first came to the Daily Show is you know…It’s a big organisation but at the same time it feels really small. So it was me hanging out with this man who I got along with and we became friends and we were laughing and having fun and we realised we are comedians who see the world in a similar way but from different points of view and so in the conversation and in the laughing he said Why don’t you … Devi: Pull in Trevor: Yes, pull in and that’s what it is…. Devi: You pulled in and stayed Devi: You’re Trevor you’re ours you belong to us. Trevor: I thought it was going to be I will always come and visit the show when I am in town. Then Jon Stewart announced he was leaving. Devi: Did you think you were in with a chance? Because you are not American you have a whole other different background? No I didn’t I approached it the same way I used to play lotto, choose my numbers, No I am not going to win you just put my ticket in the ashtray and you carry on with your life. I am not from the place where I think people will be chosen and I understand I am a strange choice. and that’s half of what life is for me I don’t expect anything but I will still put the work in to try because if you don’t try you can never get anything. V/O On the 28th September, 2015, Trevor took over the chair, his first night as host of The Daily Show. Up Sound Before we get started…… Devi: You are the boss the buck stops with you? Trevor: Yes… Devi: They sue you. Trevor: Basically I am the Guptas and everyone else is my Zumas they have to do what I say… Link If you walk down West 52 Street Hells Kitchen New York you would be forgiven if you missed that white door its quiet unimpressive but behind that door that’s where the Daily Show is put together. V/O `We spent time behind the scenes of The Daily Show, talking to the fans, seeing how their script writers and producers put the show together. Whilst the organisation is big the feeling is intimate even pets are welcomed in this space. Vox Pop V/O This Emmy award winning late night comedy talk show is all about their take on what’s happening in the news and the one constant is the morning meeting. Link Monday to Thursday the day starts at 9 am with a script writers meeting for scriptwriters where basically ideas are thrown around but the content will shape the evenings show Devi: How do you stay on top of it the news cycle is never ending. Trevor: I enjoy it you know again in a similar way I am connected to what it was like in South Africa as SA’s we take for granted how political we are on a base level so when I first came to America people said are you political and I said No I am not but then I realised what we think is not political in SA people here would think is revolutionary. Many Americans do not engage in politics at all but that’s changed now because of Donald Trump now everyone speaks about politics everyone is. Vox pop Devi: What was that first couple of weeks like because people were quiet critical others were quiet supportive? Trevor: You know the first couple of weeks were interesting because running a show is a very difficult exercise you know people take for granted it’s not hosting… I am used to hosting shows when I worked with M-Net on my show back in SA I was lucky I had started to experience what it was like to run a show so hiring writers and working with the actual production of what you are doing working through the editing etc but nothing on this scale so it was tough on the inside I didn’t have time to focus on what ws happening on the outside. V/O Midday every day, Trevor begins to review and refine the headline jokes. Around 4 in the afternoon there is rehearsal….An hour is left for rewrites until the taping of the show somewhere between 6 and 7 pm in front of a live studio audience. Link Here on the set of the Daily Show just over 200 audience members fill these seats Monday to Thursday. V/O And so every day in snow or a heat wave by 3 pm the line starts for wanna be audience members who haven’t got one of the 200 or so free tickets but are hoping for a no show….. we even found some South Africans in the line Vox Pop Devi: So the audience seems to have stabilised and you are attracting a younger audience and that’s a tough thing to do? Trevor; Yes that was the goal from the beginning, it was scary because the network said to us we want younger viewers but younger viewers don’t watch TV any more so what do you do…I had to set about doing creating a show that I believed would be interesting to people of different walks of life and ages. Devi: How different is an American audience to a SA audience Trevor: Very different… one thing is that Americans are in a space where there are a lot of conversations that are taken a lot more seriously in America than they are in SA we have many similarities don’t get me wrong you know in SA we are a lot more brash and way more honest in SA we just tell people how we feel and what we think and Americans are a lot more delicate and beat about the bush. Vox Pop V/O Trump’s presidency has been a boon for American comedy and satire…. The President only has to open his mouth…or send a tweet and there is a relentless barrage of media….Trump might be an easy target but this also means comedy has more political power than ever before for keeping the pressure on the ~President Devi: You’ve had practice you have had President Zuma Trevor: Definitely you know one thing I like about working on TDS now is that Donald Trump in many ways reminds me of JZ Trevor: UP SOUND Trevor …. both Presidents who are doing their best thing living their best life and you know people love them people hate them they both have many wives you know are not afraid of being themselves not fans of the media…there is many similarities and parallels you can draw I feel like in many ways I am familiar with the leader who is DT because he reminds me of people that we know back home. Devi: Have you extended an invite to Pres Tump Trevor: Oh yeah but we have been rejected many times Devi: You mean he even replies? Well his people reply for him it’s a NO but we keep asking week in and week out Devi: Do you sometimes sit here and pinch your self Trevor: All the time especially when I walk to work when I leave at night I don’t take any of this for granted it was never promised to me and neither is tomorrow but I am blessed that I have this today I am lucky that I have this job and its an amazing job and I get to do this every single day of my life so I don’t take that for granted at all Trevor Part 4 Devi: Nice pozzie I have to say …doorman everything. Trevor: Its funny when you move to the US you realise how many things we take for granted in SA. The space we have the type of lifestyle you can live for the amount of money you can live it and then you come to NY and you have to live a lot smaller but at the same time you’re in NY city. V/O Trevor Noah has only recently upgraded from renting to buying his New York penthouse …. for a man who works non stops it made sense to buy juts a few blocks from the The Daily Show studio. Devi And works just down the road? Trevor Yes Devi: That for me is the best part Trevor: The thing is NY traffic is insane so when I first moved here I realised the traffic was insane and in the winter time its snow so I dint know how to walk in the snow I still don’t know how to walk in the snow. Devi: and Your mom is she planning a trip? Trevor: My mom for what… Devi:For you Trevor: I must come home…you going to NY you will come home what am I doing in America No Devi: Picture her here have to entertain her Trevor: But I wouldn’t have to entertain her she does her own thing…walk…my mom has always been a free spirit that’s the nice thing about my family we talk we keep in contact but everyone is very easy in terms where we will bump into each other in the world TREVOR: I got so home sick…. Devi: Advice for young SA’s who are watching the show? The biggest advice for young SA’s is they have to break the curses of the previous generations they have to work hard not to inherit the resentments and hatreds of the previous generations. Young SA have to build whilst acknowledging the foundations of their country may be shaky,. Young SA’s have to realise its work and sometimes I think that was a message that was never given to us when 94 came and when freedom came. They said free houses for all free everything but people don’t realise that freedom is hard work I used to complain about my Mom like she was the government oppressing me. Aah this lady tells me when to sleep ha ha she doesn’t want to give me money this women telling me I must turn off the lights turn on the lights I must clean the yard I am a prisoner, a prisoner and then she said go and be free in the world and there I was going with the electricity bill I have t turn off the lights I have to pay for water pay the rent and I have to clean the house and then I realise freedom is hard work and a lot of people say they want freedom but what they are actually saying is they just don’t want to have accountability and there is a difference. Trevor Joke V/O Stand up comedy is still Trevor’s love, it’s the rapport with the audience, the often unscripted moments, and to feed his passion most weekends he travels to gigs sometimes in America sometimes further afield. Trevor’s won a number of international awards already…and just last week he received the Comedy Person of the Year Award at the ‘Just for Laughs’ Comedy Fest in Montreal. Trevor: I love stand up comedy I still love it today I been blessed enough to do it all over the world, its not easy to go from Germany to America to UK to Australia to SA not easy at all but that’s where the hard work comes in but a lot of the time people don’t see the the hard work. So they see you and go even me. I must do that but its Ya but you don’t see the work. Devi: Explain that to people they think its glamourous, we’ve shown the glamour been on set with you jump into helicopter James Bonds style its all going to be fantastic, but that’s what people see is are you getting enough sleep at night how hard are you working… Trevor:. People say WOW overnight Ya but what was happening at night I eas working and that’s where you remember to remind yourself of what your goal is and these very difficult times that come with it. But if you pace yourself and if you see life as a whole instead of little moments where your emotions are going u and down you have a broader understanding of what’s happening to you. Devi: Are you living the dream now. Trevor: Can I tell you it took me a long time to realise that that I was always living the dream. If you’re waiting to live the dream you will never live the dream. Be happy in the space that you’re in and then everything else comes to you. It’s a strange concept because people always go if I can just get the car then I will be happy; If I can just get the job then I will be happy; No be happy then let those things come to you otherwise you are mortgaging your happiness for the future. V/O This week Trevor will be back in South Africa for a series of specials and stand up comedy acts. Devi: What do you miss most about SA The people, I miss the people I miss how polite we are, how we laugh. I miss how loud we are. I miss our…the fact that we greet hello when you walk in the room. People don’t greet in America they walk right past each into rooms out of rooms they don’t care, they don’t see each other Sawubone I see you that’s all.
